content: Intermittent urethral self-dilatation is sometimes recommended as a strategy to reduce the risk of recurrent urethral stricture in males. However, there is no consensus on whether this intervention is clinically effective or cost-effective in managing the condition. This review aimed to evaluate the clinical and cost-effectiveness of intermittent self-dilatation following urethral stricture surgery in males, compared to no intervention. Additionally, it sought to compare different self-dilatation programs and devices. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials where one group underwent intermittent self-dilatation for urethral stricture. Studies that were not randomized or quasi-randomized, or those focusing on clean intermittent self-catheterization for bladder emptying, were excluded. Data collection and analysis were conducted by two authors who screened studies for relevance and methodological quality. Data extraction followed predetermined criteria, and analyses were performed using Cochrane Review Manager (RevMan 5). The primary outcomes assessed were patient-reported symptoms, health-related quality of life, and risk of recurrence. Secondary outcomes included adverse events, patient acceptability, and cost-effectiveness. The quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Eleven trials involving 776 men were included in the review. These studies were generally small, of poor quality, and had a high risk of bias. When comparing intermittent self-dilatation to no intervention, data from six trials were heterogeneous, imprecise, and biased. However, the findings suggested that men who performed intermittent self-dilatation were less likely to experience recurrent urethral stricture than those who did not (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.00; very low-quality evidence). Adverse events were poorly reported, with two trials not reporting them at all and two reporting adverse events only for the intervention group. A meta-analysis of the remaining two trials found no significant difference in adverse events between the groups (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.11 to 3.26). No trials formally assessed the acceptability of the intervention, nor did they report on patient-reported lower urinary tract symptoms, health-related quality of life, or cost-effectiveness. Two trials compared different durations of intermittent self-dilatation. One study could not draw robust conclusions due to methodological issues, including cross-over, protocol deviations, administrative errors, post-hoc analysis, and incomplete outcome reporting. The other study found no significant difference between performing intermittent self-dilatation for six months versus 12 months after optical urethrotomy (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.12 to 3.64). However, the evidence was limited by the small sample size and high risk of bias. Adverse events were reported narratively but were not stratified by group. No trials assessed acceptability, patient-reported lower urinary tract symptoms, health-related quality of life, or cost-effectiveness. Three trials compared different devices for performing intermittent self-dilatation. One trial, which had a high risk of bias, provided uncertain results regarding the effects of a low-friction hydrophilic catheter versus a standard polyvinyl chloride catheter on the risk of recurrent urethral stricture (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.40). Another study found no significant difference between using one percent triamcinolone gel versus water-based gel for catheter lubrication (RR 0.68, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.32). Two trials reported adverse events, but one did not provide sufficient detail for analysis. The other small study reported fewer instances of prostatitis, urethral bleeding, or bacteriuria with a low-friction hydrophilic catheter compared to a standard polyvinyl chloride catheter (RR 0.13, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.98). One study assessed happiness with the intervention using a non-validated scale, but no trials formally assessed patient-reported health-related quality of life or acceptability. Additionally, no trials reported on patient-reported lower urinary tract symptoms or cost-effectiveness. The evidence suggesting that intermittent self-dilatation reduces the risk of recurrent urethral stricture after surgical intervention was downgraded to very low quality due to high risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency in the data. No trials provided cost-effectiveness data or used validated patient-reported outcome measures, and adverse events were not rigorously reported. The acceptability of the intervention to patients has not been quantitatively or qualitatively assessed. In conclusion, intermittent self-dilatation may reduce the risk of recurrent urethral stricture following endoscopic treatment. However, the evidence is of very low quality, and confidence in the findings is limited. Further research is needed to determine whether the potential benefits justify the intervention and to identify the patient populations most likely to benefit.
